Photograph: Instagram View image in fullscreen Beau Lamarre-Condon is on trial for the alleged shooting murders of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in November 2024. Photograph: Instagram New South Wales Former cop Beau Lamarre-Condon argues self-defence in double murder trial citing struggle over gun Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to fatally shooting Jesse Baird, 26, and his partner, 29-year-old Luke Davies, with police service weapon in 2024 Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Kat Wong Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.53 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 22.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A former police officer claims he killed two men in self-defence and began cleaning up the crime scene because he “panicked”, a Sydney court has heard. Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting 26-year-old Jesse Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, 29, with a police service weapon at Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024. The prosecution told the supreme court on Monday that Lamarre-Condon had become infatuated and obsessed with Baird and began planning his murder in early 2024. Lamarre-Condon’s defence lawyer, John Stratton SC, told the court on Tuesday that the policeman had been acting in “self-defence”. NSW cop Beau Lamarre-Condon disguised himself as Uber Eats rider before alleged murders, court hears Read more Disguised as an Uber Eats driver, Lamarre-Condon had entered the home in a motorcycle helmet with a key he was given by Baird, Stratton said. However, Baird did not recognise Lamarre-Condon and a struggle ensued during which the 26-year-old was killed, the defence barrister told the jury. The officer’s gun was then flung across the room and Davies picked it up, Stratton told the court. Lamarre-Condon then grabbed Davies by the arm and pushed the gun towards him. In the struggle that followed, Davies pulled the trigger and shot himself, the court was told. “It’s his case that what he did was self-defence,” Stratton said. “[He was] understandably panicked. He was a police officer and he knew this looked bad.”= Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter. View image in fullscreen Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird. Composite: NSW police / Network 10 Earlier on Tuesday, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC outlined how Lamarre-Condon allegedly murdered the two men and concealed their bodies, as the trial entered its second day. The prosecution alleged Lamarre-Condon entered Baird’s house with a stolen key before shooting him twice and shooting Davies through a bedroom door. Audio of the three shots was played to the courtroom: the first two coming in quick succession before the third, 51 seconds later. Baird and Davies’ loved ones wiped away tears as they listened in court. The crown alleges that after the murders, Lamarre-Condon immediately began to clean up the crime scene and moved the bodies. He told a friend he had killed two people, the court heard. According to Hatfield, when the friend asked if he was joking, Lamarre-Condon responded: “I wish I was, I don’t feel like it was me … I feel like I need some help, this job has fucked me up.” Asked how he did it, Lamarre-Condon allegedly said “with a gun” and made a hand gesture and said “pew pew”. The friend refused to help and Lamarre-Condon later bought a second surfboard bag – days after he had bought the first, the jury was told. He returned to Baird’s home that afternoon before one of Baird’s housemates came home. “She did notice the two surfboard bags which, at this stage, were in the back courtyard,” Hatfield told the court. “She will tell you what she thought was rust [was] seeping out from the bags. She took a photo and sent it to her housemate but didn’t realise at the time that the bags contained two bodies.” A photo of outdoor furniture with a pool of blood was shown to the court on Tuesday. Lamarre-Condon would eventually buy a bag of quick set concrete and weights, and take the bags to a dam near Goulburn, the crown prosecutor said. Lamarre-Condon mixed the concrete and put it into the bags with the weights in an unsuccessful attempt to make the bodies sink, Hatfield said. He later moved the bodies to a fence line near a monastery in Bungonia where they were found eight days later, the jury was told. On Monday, Hatfield said Lamarre-Condon had developed an “infatuation and obsession” with Baird which manifested in compulsive behaviour that escalated after Baird ended their brief relationship. The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/ex-.text: The Budapest Times Ex-court president seeks ECHR ruling over politically motivated removal Péter Polt spoke on the YouTube channel called KözTér about his past as a Fidesz member, the termination of his mandate as President of the Constitutional Court, and the arrests that attracted widespread media attention. He said he had turned to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in order to receive moral redress for his removal on political grounds. The former Prosecutor General and Constitutional Court justice — whose mandate in the latter role was terminated as a result of the seventeenth amendment to the Basic Law, initiated by the Tisza government — said in the more than two-hour interview that his political background amounted to just two years of Fidesz membership, which he had left as early as 1995. He described as ignoble attacks the accusations that he had served as the Fidesz Prosecutor General or Fidesz Constitutional Court justice, noting that since the change of regime, almost every Prosecutor General had previously been a member of a political party, meaning his case was far from isolated. Regarding his forced departure from the post of President of the Constitutional Court, he said that what had happened to him was similar to what had once happened to András Baka, who had also been compelled to leave the presidency of the Supreme Court as a result of a constitutional amendment, when the apex judicial body was renamed. It is known that the current head of state — similarly to Péter Polt — also turned to the Strasbourg-based ECHR to seek justice, which ruled that the government had removed him unlawfully, in violation of the human rights convention. Péter Polt reported that he had initiated the case at the ECHR primarily to achieve “moral and ethical satisfaction,” as he believes his removal was motivated purely by political reasons. He added that he would like the ECHR to declare that the termination of his mandate was unlawful, and that he also expects some form of compensation — noting that he is basing his claim on numerous similar proceedings, not only the “Baka case,” and therefore sees good prospects for a ruling in his favour. Responding to a statement by Pál Fürcht, former head of the Central Investigation Prosecutor’s Office — who said that a superior at the Prosecutor General’s Office had verbally instructed him as to who could be investigated and who must not be questioned in the so-called gold convoy case — Péter Polt said he does not consider it conceivable that such a thing occurred. He also rejected accusations made by public figures to the effect that, as Prosecutor General, he had influenced proceedings for political reasons, stating that such actions would certainly have left traces, and no such traces exist. He added that prosecutors may only issue professional guidance — not politically motivated instructions — to the investigative authority, and that instructions can be refused if they lack a legal basis. He also cited the change in public discourse as the primary reason for the decline in public perception of the prosecution services and the chief prosecutor’s office. Regarding the appointment of Péter Fejes as chief prosecutor, he said it was a good choice, as Fejes had worked in the prosecution service for several decades and, in his view, had effectively represented the prosecution following the red sludge disaster. Responding to the observation that certain cases had been dragging on before the elections but had accelerated since April — including proceedings related to Volánbusz procurements — Péter Polt said the time had simply come for these cases. He added that the prolongation of investigative authority proceedings is not a uniquely Hungarian phenomenon, and that the prosecution phase is generally the shortest — meaning it is not the fault of the prosecuting authority that proceedings are drawn out, whether in Hungary or elsewhere. On the subject of well-known individuals and politicians being led away in custody or arrested, he said the grounds had not been made public, so he had no knowledge of whether these measures were well-founded. If they were not, however, those affected could seek legal remedy in Hungary and, later, before the ECHR as well. Regarding the work of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH), he stressed that while the establishment of the organisation is politically grounded, its integration into the justice system was not preceded by serious professional preparation. He elaborated that it is not yet clear to him why, if the NVVH can take over prosecutors and specialists, carry out tasks performed by other branches of the justice system, and requires significant financial investment, the existing institutions were not simply made more effective instead. In his view, the establishment of the NVVH cannot be justified professionally — only politically. Regarding the fact that Prime Minister Péter Magyar raised objections when his immunity was requested at the same time as that of Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták, Péter Polt said: “it is a very difficult situation when someone feels threatened” and decisions must be made under those circumstances. He added that he trusts the Hungarian justice system will be able to follow the rule-of-law path in keeping with its traditions. On the question of joining the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), he said this will further fragment the prosecutor’s office’s monopoly. In any case, it is not yet apparent to him, he said, “how much this accession will bring” for Hungary, nor is it clear what more the EPPO will offer compared to the Hungarian prosecutor’s office. In connection with the criminal proceedings against staff at child protection institutions, he highlighted that the sector has never attracted only those who wish to help, but also those who sought to exploit children, meaning there have likely always been grey areas within the system. He expressed his hope that the scandals that have recently come to light may at least serve to significantly drive back these phenomena, said Péter Polt.
